newsitem.title: USA: GM, seasonal factors seen altering jobless data.
newsitem.headline: GM, seasonal factors seen altering jobless data.

text.p: The U.S. jobless claims data due on Thursday could deviate from its main trend, distorted by the lingering effects of the now ended General Motors Corp work stoppage in Canada and by a seasonal adjustment factor, experts said.
"The story floating around is that there is likely to be a seasonal problem with the (jobless claims) numbers tomorrow," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
"The seasonal factor being used this year, compared with the seasonal used in the same week last year tends to inflate the number of claims this year," said Moran.

"Many individuals are thinking that there probably has not really been any shift in the real jobless claims trend and that therefore, this change in the seasonals will inflate the number, boosting it by about four percent," he said.
At the same time, Moran cautioned, there might be a good reason why the statistical computer program altered the seasonal factor this year, one less apparent to the naked eye.

The residual effects of U.S. layoffs related to the now concluded GM work stoppage in Canada could also taint the jobless claims data for the week ended November 2, said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.

As of November 1, 18,958 General Motors employees were still affected by the "former work stoppage in Canada," the automaker said. In addition, a truck assembly facility in Moraine, Ohio was idled on October 31 due to a lack of metal stampings from GM's Indianapolis Metal Fabricating plant where workers had gone out on strike.

The return to work on Sunday, November 3, of the Indianapolis Metal Fabricating plant and the resumption of normal operations at all the GM assembly operations affected by work stoppages in Canada and Indianapolis by Thursday, November 7, will affect next week's jobless claims data in the opposite direction, analysts said.
"The jobless claims series will probably be strike tainted this week," said Flanagan. "And so will next week's data because of a reversal effect."
Moran said the seasonal factor in play for this week's jobless claims report should push down next week's reported jobless claims figure.
"The seasonal factor will work in the opposite direction next week," he said.

Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that new jobless claims totaled 344,000 in the week ended November 2, up slightly from 342,000 new claims for state unemployment insurance filed a week earlier.
